recentItems.title: Ursula von der Leyen invites Canada to be EU's first 'associate member' | DW News
recentItems.description:
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has invited Canada to become "the first associate member of the European Union." She made the announcement during her State of the Union address, which was attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. The EU chief used her speech in Strasbourg to talk about other global threats, from climate change to AI, as well as growing geopolitical uncertainty.

00:00 Introduction
01:50 DW Analysis: What to Expect from the State of the Union
12:40 Roberta Metsola Opens the Session
15:20 Ursula von der Leyen's State of the Union Address
53:30 The Future of EU-Canada Relations
55:29 EU chief says Canada should become first "associate member"
56:50 Russia's War Against Ukraine
01:07:45 Addressing the Crisis in the Middle East
01:09:40 Migration and EU Border Security
01:14:10 Defending European Democracy
01:17:30 Social Media Rules for Children
01:23:18 The EU as a Peace Project
01:28:38 Key Takeaways and Analysis from DW's Jack Parrock

Associate member does not mean full EU membership. According to Ursula von der Leyen's announcement, it would likely mean a much closer partnership with the EU in areas such as trade, defense, technology, research and economic security, without Canada becoming an EU member state or having the same voting rights as members. The exact details have not yet been revealed because this would be a new status that currently does not exist in EU treaties.

recentItems.title: Can Germany solve America's missile problem? | DW News
recentItems.description:
After expending vast numbers of missiles during Operation Epic Fury, the United States faces a pressing challenge: rebuilding critical weapons stockpiles. Germany's Defense Minister Boris Pistorius believes he may have part of the solution: producing Tomahawk missiles in Germany.
As Pistorius meets US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington, the proposal is being presented as a potential win-win. Germany would boost its defense capabilities and support its military buildup, while the United States could accelerate missile production and replenish inventories depleted by recent operations.
Could this become a new milestone in transatlantic defense cooperation?
In this video, we speak with DW's Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is accompanying Pistorius during his visit to the United States, and with Ryan Brobst, Deputy Director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, about the strategic, political and industrial implications of the proposal.
